title: T1 — IaC with Terraform
bodyMarkdown:
## IaC with Terraform

Exam group **1**. This lesson teaches what Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is, why teams adopt it, and how Terraform's design lets one tool and one configuration language manage AWS, other clouds, and on-premises systems in the same workflow. Every fact below is backed by HashiCorp's own documentation, and each section ends with a discriminator you can use to separate the right exam answer from a close-sounding wrong one.

### tf.004.1a — Explain what IaC is

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means describing the servers, networks, and other resources you want in a file, instead of creating them by hand through a console or a one-off CLI command. HashiCorp's own definition: "Terraform is an infrastructure as code tool that lets you build, change, and version cloud and on-prem resources safely and efficiently." The files themselves are meant to be shared and reused, not just run once: you "define both cloud and on-prem resources in human-readable configuration files that you can version, reuse, and share."

Terraform's configuration files are written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), a human-readable syntax designed for describing infrastructure. HCL is declarative: "Terraform configuration files are declarative, meaning that they describe the end state of your infrastructure." A declarative file states what should exist (for example, "one EC2 instance of this type, in this subnet") and leaves the ordering and API calls needed to get there to Terraform. This is different from an imperative script, which lists the exact ordered steps an operator or program must run (create the VPC, then the subnet, then the instance) to reach that same state.

The discriminator the exam leans on: manual provisioning through a console click-path or a one-off CLI command is not IaC, because there is no file to review, diff, version, or re-run; the same clicks have to be repeated by hand next time, and nothing records what was actually done. A configuration file committed to version control is IaC, whether or not it happens to be declarative. Terraform specifically is also declarative IaC, which is the second half of the distinction the exam tests: IaC versus manual work is about whether infrastructure is defined in a file at all, while declarative versus imperative is about whether that file states an end goal (Terraform's approach) or a sequence of steps (a shell script calling a cloud CLI in order).

**Exam tip:** if a scenario says the same manual console steps are repeated by hand every time, or an operator remembers "what to click," that is not IaC; if a scenario says a file defines the desired resources and is checked into version control, that is IaC, and if that file lists an end state rather than ordered steps, it is also declarative.

### tf.004.1b — Describe the advantages of IaC patterns

Terraform's documentation lists specific advantages IaC provides over the manual and imperative-scripting alternative from 1a, and each one maps to a concrete Terraform mechanism.

The first advantage is a consistent workflow across the whole resource lifecycle: you "use a consistent workflow to provision and manage all of your infrastructure throughout its lifecycle," so creating, changing, and removing a resource all go through the same steps instead of a different manual procedure for each. The second is efficiency through parallel execution: "Terraform builds a resource graph to determine resource dependencies and creates or modifies non-dependent resources in parallel." A hand-written imperative script normally runs its steps in the exact order they were written, even when two resources have nothing to do with each other; Terraform's resource graph works out which resources actually depend on which, so unrelated resources can be created at the same time without a person hand-ordering the script. The third advantage is tracking: "Terraform keeps track of your real infrastructure in a state file, which acts as a source of truth for your environment," so Terraform (not the operator's memory) knows what already exists before it changes anything; this state file is covered in full in objective 2d. The fourth is collaboration: teams "commit it to a Version Control System (VCS) and use HCP Terraform to efficiently manage Terraform workflows across teams," which turns an infrastructure change into something that can be reviewed like any other code change before it is applied.

The discriminator: a plain automation script that wraps a cloud vendor's CLI in a loop is still code, and it can be repeatable, but by itself it usually has no tracked record of what it already created, so re-running it can duplicate resources or fail confusingly, and there is no resource graph deciding what is safe to run in parallel. An IaC pattern like Terraform's adds the tracked state and dependency graph on top of "it's just a script," which is what actually delivers the safety and parallelism advantages, not the mere fact that a script exists.

**Exam tip:** if a stem's benefit is "the same steps work for creating, changing, or removing infrastructure" or "independent resources are provisioned at the same time without manual ordering," that is a Terraform IaC-pattern advantage; a benefit that only claims "it's automated" without tracked state or a dependency graph is a weaker, generic-scripting answer.

### tf.004.1c — Explain how Terraform manages multi-cloud, hybrid cloud, and service-agnostic workflows

Terraform's multi-cloud reach comes from its provider plugin model, not from Terraform itself knowing about every platform. "Providers enable Terraform to work with virtually any platform or service with an accessible API," and published providers for most platforms are listed in the Terraform Registry. A provider is the plugin that translates Terraform's generic resource and data block syntax into the specific API calls a given platform (AWS, another cloud, an on-premises system, or a SaaS product like a DNS registrar) understands; "service-agnostic" means Terraform's core workflow does not care which kind of service a provider talks to, as long as that service exposes an API a provider can call.

This is the direct contrast HashiCorp draws with a cloud-specific provisioning tool such as AWS CloudFormation. CloudFormation's own engine and template syntax only understand AWS resources. Terraform's provider model instead lets one configuration and one workflow span multiple platforms at once: "Terraform can be used to orchestrate an AWS and OpenStack cluster simultaneously, while enabling 3rd-party providers like Cloudflare and DNSimple." Instead of learning a different tool per platform, "it provides a single unified syntax, instead of requiring operators to use independent and non-interoperable tools for each platform and service," which is what lets "Terraform represent and manage the entire infrastructure with its supporting services, instead of only the subset that exists within a single provider." That single syntax and single workflow, applied across whichever providers a configuration declares, is also how Terraform handles a hybrid-cloud scenario: one AWS provider block and one on-premises or VMware provider block can sit in the same configuration and be applied through the same workflow.

The discriminator: if a scenario requires provisioning AWS and Azure resources, or AWS and an on-premises system, from the same configuration language and the same workflow, that need points to Terraform's provider model, not to a single-cloud native tool whose syntax cannot express another vendor's resources at all. A tool built for one platform can still be excellent at that platform; it is simply not the answer when the requirement explicitly spans more than one provider or environment.

**Exam tip:** "one tool, one workflow, multiple clouds or an on-prem system in the same configuration" is Terraform's provider-agnostic model; a requirement that only ever names a single cloud vendor's native tool is not testing this objective.

### Warnings

- Do not run `terraform apply` or `terraform destroy` against real cloud credentials in this workbook; only `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate` are safe to run freely.
- Never call `ExecuteTerraformCommand` or `ExecuteTerragruntCommand` from this workbook's tools.
- A local Terraform state file can hold sensitive values in plain text; never commit it to a public repository.
